newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Turkmen red tape hampers aid for Afghan refugees.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen red tape hampers aid for Afghan refugees.

text.p: Turkmen bureaucracy is thwarting the timely provision of aid to some 8,000 Afghan refugees who fled to Turkmenistan last week to escape fighting in northern Afghanistan, a senior relief official said on Tuesday.

Eric Michel-Selier, regional delegate for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, said Afghan refugees allowed by Turkmen authorities into the country were facing severe shortages of food and drinking water.
"But when I wanted to buy wheat flour for the refugees, the local governor could not take the decision," Michel-Selier told Reuters by satellite phone from Turkmenistan.
"I feel that Turkmen authorities just want the refugees to return to Afghanistan as quickly as possibly," he added.
Thorir Gudmundsson, the federation's regional information delegate, told Reuters in the Kazakh capital Almaty that bureaucracy in secretive Turkmenistan was the main problem.

"Everything in Turkmenistan is resolved in the capital Ashgabat and you cannot take decisions locally," he said. "We expect trucks with food and medicines to arrive shortly from Tajikistan which they must be leaving tomorrow (Wednesday) morning."

The refugees fled from the town of Mari Chak on the Afghan side of the Murgab river, which separates the two states, to escape fighting in northern Afghanistan where forces of the purist Taleban militia are pitted against troops of Uzbek General Abdul Malik.
The Taleban are battling to regain control of territories in the north they briefly won and then lost to the anti-Taleban alliance in May.
Several hundred metres (yards) separate the refugee camps from the Murgab river. Michel-Selier said that on Monday evening the Taleban had shouted something from the other side.
"It seems that the Taleban were shouting that the refugees must return," he said. But the refugees seem to prefer staying in inhospitable Turkmenistan.
"They say they do not want to return and are very scared by the Taleban. Some old people say: 'We prefer to die instead of returning to Afghanistan'," Michel-Selier said.

The former Soviet republics neighbouring Afghanistan have voiced concern that fighting there could trigger an exodus of civilians. The refugees at Takhta Bazar are the first major influx of displaced Afghans to one of the ex-Soviet Central Asian states.
